idiom_name: staged chain with runtime guards (no checker rejects a skipped step)
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no static checker, so the pattern's defining promise - the misordered or incomplete construction does not compile - cannot be delivered: a chain of step objects can be written, but every guarantee is a runtime check that fires (or does not) only on the path that executes. The idiomatic answer to construction with required and optional settings is a single options object whose required members are validated once at the boundary: destructuring with defaults for the optional ones, an explicit check (or node:assert, or a schema validator) for the required ones. Keep a staged chain only when the API is consumed by untyped callers and the order of side effects genuinely matters; then validate in the terminal build() and throw a message naming the missing or misordered step.
pitfalls: Destructuring and default parameters never fail on a missing key, so a 'required' option silently becomes undefined and the failure surfaces at the next consumer instead of the call site.
With no type checker, renaming or reordering a step leaves call sites that break only when that path runs - a staged chain looks safer than it is and hides this from reviews.
The builder mutates one shared object; captured in a closure or a module-level singleton, two concurrent constructions interleave, and an abandoned chain leaves partial state behind.
alternative: A single options object (or a config record) with documented defaults and one up-front validation of the required members - destructuring defaults plus an explicit check, node:assert, or a schema validator; when the guarantee must be static, move the call site to TypeScript and use the generic staged builder there.
